{{Politics of Scotland}}

For [[Local government in Scotland|local government]] purposes, [[Scotland]] is divided into 32 areas designated as "council areas" ({{langx|gd|comhairlean}}), which are all governed by [[unitary authority|single-tier authorities]] designated as "councils".<ref>{{Cite web |title=Local government facts and figures: Scotland |url=https://lgiu.org/local-government-facts-and-figures-scotland/ |access-date=2022-03-14 |website=lgiu.org |language=en-GB}}</ref> They have the option under the Local Government (Gaelic Names) (Scotland) Act 1997<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.opsi.gov.uk/acts/acts1997/1997006.htm|title=Local Government (Gaelic Names) (Scotland) Act 1997}}</ref> of being known (but not re-designated) as a "''comhairle''" when opting for a Gaelic name; only ''[[Comhairle nan Eilean Siar]]'' (Council of the Western Isles) has chosen this option, whereas the [[Highland Council]] (''Comhairle na Gàidhealtachd'') has adopted its Gaelic form alongside its English equivalent, informally.

The council areas have been in existence since 1 April 1996, under the provisions of the [[Local Government etc. (Scotland) Act 1994]]. Historically, Scotland was divided into 34 [[Shires of Scotland|counties or shires]]. Although these no longer have any administrative function, they are still used to some extent in Scotland for cultural and geographical purposes, and some of the current council areas are named after them. There are also a number of other administrative divisions, some of which are handled by joint boards of the councils.

At the most local level, Scotland is divided into [[List of civil parishes in Scotland|civil parishes]], which are now used only for statistical purposes such as the census. The lowest level of administrative subdivision are the [[community council|communities]], which may elect ''community councils''.

==History of the subdivisions of Scotland==
{{further|Burgh#History|History of local government in Scotland}}

Traditionally burghs have been the key unit of the [[Local government in Scotland|local government of Scotland]], being highly [[Autonomous entity|autonomous]] entities, with rights to representation in the old [[Parliament of Scotland]]. Even after the [[Acts of Union 1707]], burghs continued to be the principal subdivision. Until 1889, administration was on a [[burgh]] and [[parish]] basis.

The years following 1889 saw the introduction of a hierarchy of local government administration comprising [[Counties of Scotland|counties]], [[Local Government (Scotland) Act 1889|counties of cities]], [[large burghs]] and small burghs.

With effect from 16 May 1975 and until 31 March 1996 the local government divisions of Scotland consisted of an upper tier of ''[[Regions and districts of Scotland|regions]]'' each containing a lower tier of ''[[Regions and districts of Scotland|districts]]'' except for the single-tier ''[[Island council areas of Scotland|island council areas]]''. Since 1996 there has only been a single tier of government, and the former island council areas are of equal status to the other councils.

==Other subdivisions==
Scotland has several other administrative divisions, some of which are handled by joint boards of the councils.

===Electoral and valuation===
There are several joint boards for [[Electoral registration in the United Kingdom|electoral registration]] and the purposes of property valuation for assessing [[council tax]] and [[rates (tax)|rates]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.saa.gov.uk/|title=Scottish Assessors – Scottish Assessors Association website}}</ref>

===Land registration===
The current [[Registers of Scotland|land registration system]] in Scotland divides Scotland into 33 [[Registration county#Scotland|Registration Counties]],<ref>Registers of Scotland publication - Land Register Counties and Operational Dates</ref> each coming into effect on various dates between 1981 and 2003. These areas in most cases resemble those of the pre-1975 administrative counties with Glasgow being the only current city to form a registration county.

===Lieutenancy areas===
The [[Lieutenancy areas of Scotland]] are the areas used for the ceremonial [[Lord Lieutenant|lord-lieutenants]], the [[British monarch|monarch]]'s representatives.  The areas are similar to the Historic Counties and the Registration Counties, but are not identical to either.  Most notably, the four cities of [[Aberdeen]], [[Dundee]], [[Edinburgh]], and [[Glasgow]] form separate areas from the surrounding countryside, with the [[Lord Provost]] of each city acting ''[[ex officio]]'' as the lord-lieutenant.

=== Former police and fire services ===
The Police and Fire Reform (Scotland) Act 2012 resulted in the merger of local [[police]] and [[fire department|fire services]] on 1 April 2013 to form the [[Police Scotland|Police Service of Scotland]] ([[Scottish Gaelic]]: {{lang|gd|Seirbheis Phoilis na h-Alba}}) and the [[Scottish Fire and Rescue Service]] (SFRS, Scottish Gaelic: {{lang|gd|Seirbheis Smàlaidh agus Teasairginn na h-Alba}}).

Prior to 1975 policing was the responsibility of the Cities and Burghs of Scotland (see [[List of burghs in Scotland]]).  Between 1975 and 2013 Scotland was subdivided into [[Police]] and [[firefighter|fire]] service areas based on the [[regions and districts (Scotland)|regions and districts]] and [[island council areas (Scotland)|island council areas]] that were also formed in 1975. The police and fire service regions used between 1975 and 2013 are listed below.

==Lower level subdivisions==
{{see also|Local government in Scotland}}
Scotland is divided into [[List of civil parishes in Scotland|871 civil parishes]] which often resemble same-named but legally different ecclesiastical parishes. Although they have had no administrative function since 1930, they still exist and are still used for statistical purposes such as the census. Many former civil parish areas also continued to form [[registration district]]s until 1 January 2007. Many boundary changes have occurred over the years and an area currently derived from an old parish might no longer contain a place previously within that parish. Similarly, county boundaries (as still used for land registration) have also changed over the years such that a parish mentioned historically (generally before the 1860s) as being in one county (or sometimes two due to straddling a border) might now be in a neighbouring county and consequentially in a different succeeding council area.

For most administrative purposes, the base level of sub-division in Scotland is now that of [[Community council|communities]], which may elect ''community councils''. The main role of these bodies is to channel and reflect local opinion to other bodies; they otherwise have very limited powers. There are around 1,200 communities in Scotland. Not all communities have councils; some have joint councils.

Scottish communities are the nearest equivalent to [[civil parishes in England|civil parish]]es in England.
